identity.name: Wikidata / Wikibase
identity.originator: Wikimedia Foundation / Wikimedia Deutschland. Key figures: Denny Vrandecic (founder), Lydia Pintscher (portfolio lead)
identity.year: 2012 (Wikidata launch). Wikibase software first released alongside Wikidata.
identity.key_text: Wikidata: A Free Collaborative Knowledgebase (Vrandecic & Krotzsch, 2014, Communications of the ACM)

conceptual.core_claim: A free, collaborative, multilingual knowledge graph that anyone can edit, serving as central structured data storage for Wikimedia projects and beyond, with community-governed ontology evolution.
conceptual.relation_to_attention_economy: Wikidata explicitly refuses attention-driven design — no algorithmic feeds, no engagement optimization. However, its integration with Wikipedia means it indirectly shapes what gets surfaced by search engines and AI systems. The knowledge graph's structure influences LLM training data, creating a quiet but powerful attention-shaping effect that is unacknowledged in its governance model.
conceptual.relation_to_commons: The strongest commons model among existing knowledge graphs. CC0 licensing. Community-governed with transparent decision processes. Recognized as a Digital Public Good (2025). However, the commons governance struggles with scale — 116 million items create governance challenges that push toward technocratic solutions.
conceptual.epistemological_stance: [uncertain] Empirical-consensus hybrid. Knowledge validity is determined by community consensus backed by cited sources. Multiple statements can coexist (with qualifiers and references), but the social process tends toward convergence on 'correct' values. Uncertainty is representable through qualifiers but culturally undervalued.

technical.architecture_pattern: Centralized knowledge graph with federated query capability (SPARQL federation). Item-property-value triples with qualifiers, references, and ranks. Wikibase software can be self-hosted for independent instances.
technical.data_model: Entity-centric: Items (Q-numbers) connected by Properties (P-numbers) to values. Values can be other items, strings, quantities, coordinates, dates, etc. Qualifiers add context to statements. References track provenance. Ranks indicate preferred/normal/deprecated status.
technical.temporal_logic: Bi-temporal by design. Statements can have start/end date qualifiers. Historical and current data coexist. However, temporal reasoning is not native — it requires SPARQL queries to reconstruct timelines. No anticipatory or cyclical temporal logic.
technical.absence_handling: No structural absence detection. Missing data is simply absent — there is no mechanism to flag what should exist but doesn't. WikiProjects manually identify coverage gaps, but this is social rather than computational. The constraint system (EntitySchemas, ShEx) can validate what exists but cannot diagnose what is missing.
technical.scalability_model: Centralized with federation aspirations. 116 million items, 16 billion triples. Blazegraph backend is under severe stress. The 2025-2028 development plan focuses on federated SPARQL and the Wikibase ecosystem, but true federation remains aspirational. Self-hosted Wikibase instances are operationally independent.

garden_logic_comparative.layer_mapping: substrate + participation — Wikidata provides both data infrastructure (substrate) and a community contribution model (participation). It does not have a sensing loop or prompt-generation layer.
garden_logic_comparative.intention_vs_attention: Neither optimally. Wikidata is designed for reference — answering factual queries. It does not diagnose structural gaps (intention) or optimize for engagement (attention). It optimizes for coverage — making as many facts as possible available. This is a third mode: encyclopedic completeness. A(DAI) should note that completeness is a trap for the garden — the goal is not to know everything but to sense what matters.
garden_logic_comparative.coherence_vs_consensus: Strong consensus orientation. The community process drives toward agreed-upon values. While multiple statements can technically coexist (with different ranks), the social norm is to resolve disagreements. Deprecated rank is used to mark superseded claims. This is not coherence in A(DAI)'s sense — contested readings are not first-class. However, the qualifier system hints at what coherence infrastructure could look like: a statement with qualifiers like 'according to source X' and 'disputed by source Y' approaches contestable knowledge.
garden_logic_comparative.contestability: Moderate. Any editor can contest any statement. Edit wars are mediated through community processes. However, the contestation is oriented toward resolving disputes, not preserving productive tension. There is no 'contested edge' status that remains visible to downstream consumers.
garden_logic_comparative.forkability: High for data (CC0 license), moderate for infrastructure. Anyone can download and fork the entire dataset. Wikibase software enables sovereign instances. However, the network effects of the central Wikidata instance create gravitational pull that makes forks practically marginal. No provenance tracking across forks — a forked dataset loses its connection to the living community process.
garden_logic_comparative.tendency_axis_position: openness: maximally open (CC0) | commons: strong commons (community-governed, no extraction) | spectacle: infrastructure (no engagement layer) | individual: distributed contribution, centralized aggregation
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_adopt: The qualifier and reference system as a model for provenance-rich assertions. The ability to attach 'according to whom' and 'as of when' to every edge is exactly what A(DAI)'s merge boundary needs. The EntitySchema/ShEx validation pattern for defining structural expectations on node types. The multilingual architecture — A(DAI) will need this as scenes are global. The Wikibase self-hosting model as evidence that federated sovereignty is possible with shared infrastructure.
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_refuse: The consensus-resolution social process. A(DAI) must keep contested edges visible, not resolve them. The encyclopedic completeness goal — the garden should be selective and intentional about what it indexes. The centralized SPARQL endpoint model — A(DAI)'s CR-SQLite architecture prioritizes forkability over query power for good reason. The anonymous editing model — A(DAI) needs attributed provenance on every contribution.
garden_logic_comparative.structural_tension: [uncertain] The deepest tension is between community governance and category emergence. Wikidata's ontology evolves through community proposals and votes — a democratic process that works for stable categories but struggles with frontier concepts. When someone proposes a property for a practice that doesn't have consensus vocabulary yet, the community process either rejects it (too niche) or forces premature naming (consensus before understanding). A(DAI)'s Mode B3 (vocabulary proposals) faces the same challenge: how do you govern categories that are still forming? Wikidata's experience suggests that community governance works for the middle of the distribution but fails at the edges — precisely where A(DAI) operates.

critical.limits: Severe scalability crisis. 116M items strain Blazegraph. Query timeouts are common for complex SPARQL. Ontological inconsistencies accumulate faster than they can be resolved — disjointness violations documented by researchers. The gap between the formal data model (which allows nuanced statements) and the social practice (which trends toward simple assertions) means the model's full expressive power is rarely used.
critical.who_is_excluded: [uncertain] Non-English-speaking communities are underrepresented despite the multilingual architecture. The Global South has fewer editors and fewer items. People and practices without Wikipedia articles are less likely to have Wikidata items. The editing community is predominantly male, technically literate, and Western. Indigenous knowledge systems that resist itemization into discrete facts are structurally excluded.
critical.failure_under_attention: [uncertain] If the attention economy leaks in, Wikidata becomes a battlefield for reputation management. We already see this: corporate and political actors edit items to shape how they appear in Google Knowledge Panels and LLM training data. The CC0 license means extracted data cannot be protected. AI companies already bulk-harvest Wikidata for training, extracting value from community labor without reciprocity.

governance.governance_model: Polycentric commons. The Wikimedia Foundation provides infrastructure. The community governs content through policies, guidelines, and consensus processes. Property proposals require community approval. No single authority controls the ontology, but the Foundation controls the infrastructure.
governance.consent_architecture: [uncertain] Opt-in for contributors (anyone can choose to edit). No consent mechanism for subjects — a living artist described in Wikidata has no formal way to contest their representation or opt out. GDPR right to erasure creates tension with the project's completeness goals. Machine-readable consent is absent.

materiality.extraction_vector: [uncertain] Extracts volunteer labor at massive scale. The CC0 license enables unlimited commercial extraction without reciprocity — Google, Apple, and AI companies use Wikidata extensively. The volunteers create value; the extractors capture it. The Wikimedia Foundation mediates but does not prevent extraction.
materiality.composability: Highly composable. CC0 data can be embedded anywhere. SPARQL endpoint enables programmatic access. Wikibase is self-hostable. JSON/RDF exports available. Mix-and-match with other ontologies via federated SPARQL. API-first and protocol-level.
materiality.liveness: Extremely active. Thousands of edits per hour. Continuous community governance. 2025-2028 development plan recently published. Recognized as Digital Public Good in 2025. Growing ecosystem of Wikibase instances.
materiality.scale_of_operation: Planetary. 116 million items. Multilingual. Used by search engines, AI systems, Wikipedia, and thousands of downstream applications. The largest open knowledge graph in existence.
materiality.temporality: Bi-temporal (statements with date qualifiers can represent both historical and current facts). Archives change history through edit logs. No anticipatory or cyclical temporal logic. Deep historical coverage but present-focused editing practice.
